26727-the-political-history-of-england-v:
The Honorable George C. Brodrick, late warden of Merton College, Oxford, wrote this volume of The Political History of England, completed and revised by J. K. Fotheringham, and published by Longmans, Green and Company. Editors William Hunt and Reginald L. Poole planned twelve volumes by twelve writers, each a separate complete book with its own index and maps. This eleventh volume runs from Addington's administration to the close of William the Fourth's reign.

The series preface notes seventy-five years since Lingard completed his history at the Revolution of 1688, with new materials and old errors corrected. Politics comes first, with religious, intellectual, social, and economic progress noticed alongside. A sampled passage counts Waterloo-era forces at sixty-seven thousand six hundred and sixty-one effective men against Napoleon's seventy-two thousand, stronger in cavalry and guns, the flower of the French army.
36783-concerning-lafcadio-hearn-with-a-b:
Concerning Lafcadio Hearn, by George Gould, was published in London in 1908, with a bibliography by Laura Stedman. Five pictures go with the book, including a photograph of Hearn from 1889 at the front, Hearn at about age eight, and Hearn at Martinique in 1888. A page of his handwriting is also shown.

Contents open with heredity and the early life, then Hearn in person. The period of the gruesome, the New Orleans time, and Martinique follow. Getting a soul, in ghostly Japan, Hearn as a poet, and the poet of myopia come next. Hearn style gets its own chapter, then a summary and conclusion. Appreciations and epitomes run to more than a hundred pages, and the bibliography follows. Chapter one notes that many conflicting accounts exist of Hearn parents and childhood. Readers get an early life and work study of a singular writer.
podcast-joerogan-FM463bp-UdM:
Comic Brian Simpson joins Joe Rogan for episode 2414 of the Joe Rogan Experience. Simpson, a Marine veteran turned stand-up, built a following with sharp, dark takes on race, family, and life. His star was rising fast when this hour was recorded.

Simpson tells stories from his rough Texas upbringing and his road through the comedy clubs. He and Rogan trade views on fatherhood, discipline, and the state of stand-up. The humor stays dry and cutting throughout. Laughing night owls get a strong new voice, unfiltered, in the big chair.
